name: 英洋軒 姫路駅前店 (Eiyoken Himeji Ekimae)

claims.text: Small open kitchen with no separation between gyoza (wheat wrappers) and other items; cross-contamination must be assumed.
Banshu soy sauce (播州しょうゆ) is explicitly cited as a core seasoning — this is standard wheat-containing Japanese soy sauce.
All dishes involve pork (gyoza filling), chicken (karaage), or egg (omelette); no plant-only cooking surfaces or ingredients documented.
No allergen information is published and no allergy-handling procedures are documented. Staff communication is entirely in Japanese.

name: 驛麺 らぁ～めん京 山陽姫路駅店 (Ekimen Ramen Kyo Sanyo-Himeji Station)

claims.text: Wheat noodles are cooked in shared water; gyoza, ramen, and rice-bowl items with soy-sauce-based sauces all share the same small kitchen. No allergen separation is described anywhere.
Soy-sauce tare (醤油ダレ) is a base component of the broth; conventional Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. The official site describes the soup as 鶏ガラ豚骨醤油スープ.
Every broth contains animal products (chicken bone, pork bone, or dashi); there is no plant-based option and therefore no vegan-safe item on the menu.

Tabelog notes アレルギー表示あり (allergy information available), suggesting customers should inquire directly at the restaurant (TEL: 079-223-5875), but no protocol or allergen sheet is documented in any fetched source.

Building owner Tanabiki Seimen is a wheat noodle (somen) manufacturer; noodle-based dishes are served in the space. Cross-contamination risk from wheat flour in a shared kitchen environment cannot be ruled out.
Obanzai-style Japanese home cooking (the anchor tenant's specialty) routinely uses wheat-based soy sauce and mirin. No gluten-free soy sauce alternative has been confirmed by any vendor.

No vendor has published vegan certification or confirmed separation of animal and plant ingredients. Japanese dashi (fish or bonito stock) is standard in obanzai cooking and is not explicitly excluded.

No allergen menu or staff allergy-handling protocol has been published by any rotating tenant. Contact the specific vendor operating on your planned visit day via Instagram (@cafe_eni_himeji) well in advance.
The anchor tenant obann emphasizes organic, pesticide-free vegetables and a 'body-kind' cooking philosophy, suggesting some sensitivity to ingredient quality and dietary awareness.
Vegetable-forward menus and seasonal produce are consistently highlighted across multiple tenants, indicating plant-based options are likely available on most days.

name: ごはんとおバンザイ ジグザグ (Gohan to Obanzai Ziguzagu)

claims.text: No dedicated GF fryer or preparation area is mentioned in any source. Fried items (e.g. fried chicken) appear on the rotating obanzai menu, making shared-fryer cross-contamination a realistic concern.
Standard Japanese soy sauce (shoyu, containing wheat) is a baseline ingredient in obanzai cooking; no tamari or wheat-free soy sauce alternatives are mentioned anywhere.
Miso soup dashi is prepared daily and described as rich-flavoured, most likely containing bonito (katsuo). Meat and fish dishes share the kitchen with vegetable obanzai; no separation is noted.
No sources mention staff allergy training, allergen menus, or any protocol for dietary requests. Lunch operates without reservations, limiting pre-visit communication.
The menu is built around seasonal vegetables, with roughly 10 of the 16 daily dishes being vegetable-based, giving plant-leaning diners more choice than a typical teishoku restaurant.
Fried items (chikuwa isobe-age) are listed on the menu with no mention of a dedicated fryer or GF protocols. Cross-contamination with wheat via shared frying oil is likely.
No allergen menu exists. Standard wheat-containing soy sauce is expected throughout izakaya cooking — in sauces, dipping broths, marinades, and oden tare.
Oden broth and most cooked dishes at a traditional izakaya rely on katsuobushi (bonito flake) dashi. No plant-based broth option is documented.

No allergy menu, staff allergy training, or special dietary accommodation policy has been documented for this restaurant. The owner-operated format means direct conversation with Saito Eriko at the counter is the only route to clarifying ingredients.
Counter seating directly in front of the owner allows for direct, personal conversation about ingredients — easier than at a larger izakaya chain.
Sashimi (fresh fish and local chicken tataki) are naturally wheat-free in their base form, though dipping sauces (ponzu, soy) typically contain wheat.

name: 餃子のかっちゃん 姫路駅前2号店 (Gyoza no Kacchan Himeji Ekimae Branch 2)

claims.text: Standard wheat-flour gyoza wrappers are made and cooked on-site daily; karaage (fried chicken) is a signature menu item using wheat-flour coating. Wheat contamination risk is pervasive throughout the kitchen.
Soy sauce (which contains wheat) is served tableside as a dipping condiment for gyoza and is almost certainly used in cooking sauces. No tamari or wheat-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned.
Pork is present in the core gyoza product and horse meat (馬刺しユッケ) and fried chicken are on the menu; shared cooking surfaces and fryers make vegan cross-contact highly likely.
No allergen menu, allergy-handling protocol, or staff allergy training is mentioned in any available source. Inquiries would need to be made in Japanese by phone (079-280-1202).

Small izakaya kitchen serving fried dishes (karaage, anago tempura, tuna-skin karaage) alongside non-fried items. No dedicated fryer confirmed; shared-oil cross-contamination with wheat-coated items is likely.

Wheat-based soy sauce is central to virtually all cooking here: oden broth, sashimi dipping sauce, marinades for grilled anago, and karaage batter all conventionally contain wheat. No tamari or gluten-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned anywhere.

Fish dashi is the backbone of Himeji oden and likely used in multiple dishes. Shared cooking surfaces in a small kitchen handling fish, shellfish, and meat throughout service make vegan isolation impractical without direct advance arrangement.

No allergy-handling policy, allergen menu, or dietary accommodation statement is published on the official site, Tabelog, HotPepper, or Gurunavi listings. Direct phone inquiry (079-224-3999) before visiting is strongly advised for any dietary restriction.

Fresh seafood sourced directly from Murotsu fishing port means dishes are made to order rather than pre-processed, which in principle allows ingredient-level discussion with staff for guests who can communicate in Japanese.

name: はまもとコーヒー (Hamamoto Coffee)

claims.text: No dedicated GF preparation area or allergen segregation noted anywhere. This is a bread-and-toast-centric kissaten; wheat flour is central to the menu and cross-contamination must be assumed.
No soy sauce in the menu items identified. Coffee shop menu (coffee, toast, egg) does not appear to use soy sauce. However, no allergen declaration is publicly available.
Eggs and dairy (almond butter spread) are used in core menu items throughout the kitchen; no plant-based separation noted.
No allergy handling policy, allergen menu, or staff allergy training information was found across any source. Phone contact (079-282-2233) is the only avenue to inquire.

Siphon-brewed black coffee (no milk, no soy sauce, no gluten ingredients) is naturally gluten-free and vegan as a standalone item — the safest choice for restricted diners who want to experience the shop.
